findings.finding: My current finding is that the cross‑correlation condition forces the set of shift values where the dot product is non‑zero to be exactly the set of differences between indices of $\alpha$’s support $\{0,\dots,8\}$ and indices of $\beta$’s support $I$. Thus, for a shifty $\alpha$ we must have $I$ such that the difference set $\{j-i:j\in[0,8],\,i\in I\}$ contains precisely two integers $k$ and $l$, and for each of those the weighted sum $\sum_{i\in I}\beta(i)\alpha(i+n)=1$. This reduces the problem to finding integer pairs $(\alpha,\beta)$ where the difference set of their supports has size two and the corresponding weighted sums equal one.

My current finding is that the problem reduces to finding Laurent polynomials $A(t)=\sum_{i=0}^8\alpha(i)t^i$ and $B(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\beta(j)t^j$ with integer coefficients such that $A(t)B(t)=t^k+t^l$ for some distinct integers $k,l$.  Thus a shifty $\alpha$ exists iff its polynomial $A(t)$ is a divisor of the binomial $t^k+t^l$ in $\mathbb Z[t,t^{-1}]$.  This turns the counting problem into counting integer‑coefficient divisors of $t^k+t^l$ with support in $\{0,\dots,8\}$.

My current finding is that for any shifty $\alpha$ the cross‑correlation $f(n)=S_n(\alpha)\star\beta$ must be a finite sequence with support exactly $\{k,l\}$.  Since $\alpha$ is supported on $\{0,\dots,8\}$ and $\beta$ on some finite set, $f$ is automatically supported in a bounded interval.  Thus the existence of $\beta$ reduces to solving a linear system of equations over $\mathbb Z$ with $9$ unknowns $\alpha_0,\dots,\alpha_8$ and finitely many equations $f(n)=\delta_{n,k}+\delta_{n,l}$.  This shows the problem is equivalent to finding integer vectors $\alpha$ that are orthogonal to all but two shifts of some integer vector $\beta$.

My current finding is that the problem reduces to finding integer polynomials \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^8 a_i x^i\) and \(B(x)=\sum_j b_j x^j\) (with \(b_j=\beta(-j)\)) such that \(A(x)B(x)=x^k+x^l\). This is equivalent to a factorization of the binomial \(x^k+x^l=x^l(1+x^{k-l})\) into two integer polynomials with one factor supported in \([0,8]\). Thus the number of shifty \(\alpha\) equals the number of ways to factor \(1+x^m\) (with \(m=|k-l|>0\)) into two integer polynomials where one factor has degree ≤8. This gives a concrete finite search space.

My current finding is that the condition on α and β is equivalent to a factorisation of the polynomial \(z^{k}+z^{l}\) over the integers: if we let \(A(z)=\sum_{t=0}^{8}\alpha(t)z^{t}\) and \(B'(z)=\sum_{m} \beta(-m)z^{m}\), then the cross‑correlation equation becomes \(A(z)B'(z)=z^{k}+z^{l}\). Thus a shifty α exists iff there is an integer polynomial \(A(z)\) with degree ≤ 8 that divides a binomial \(z^{k}+z^{l}\) (with \(k\neq l\)). This reduces the problem to counting integer divisors of such binomials whose degree is at most 8.

My current finding is that a shifty function α must satisfy a polynomial factorisation: if we write \(A(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{8}\alpha(i)x^i\) and let \(G(x)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\beta(j)x^j\) (a Laurent polynomial), then the convolution condition is equivalent to \(A(x)G(x)=x^k+x^l\) for distinct integers \(k,l\). Thus \(A(x)\) must be a divisor of a binomial \(x^k+x^l\) in \(\mathbb Z[x,x^{-1}]\). Since units in this ring are \(\pm x^m\), the only possible non‑unit divisors are the cyclotomic polynomials \(\Phi_d(x)\) that divide \(x^k+x^l\). This reduces the search for α to checking which 9‑term polynomials (with integer coefficients) are such cyclotomic factors, giving a finite list to enumerate.

My current finding is that a shifty function α must have support in \([0,8]\) and that the convolution map \(T_\alpha:\gamma\mapsto\alpha*\gamma\) generates all sequences that are ℤ‑linear combinations of shifts of α. Thus a shifty α exists iff the indicator \(e_k+e_l\) lies in the ℤ‑span of \(\{S_m\alpha:m\in\mathbb Z\}\). This reduces the problem to checking whether the two‑point sequence can be expressed as a finite integer linear combination of shifts of α. No closed form yet, but it shows the problem is equivalent to a lattice‑span condition.

My current finding is that any “single‑delta” function α(t)=±1 at a single integer m∈[0,8] satisfies the shifty condition: choose β(t)=±(δ_{m−k}+δ_{m−l}) with the same sign as α, then S_nα⋆β=1 exactly at n=k,l and 0 elsewhere. This gives 2·9=18 shifty functions from the 9 possible m and two signs. I have not yet ruled out other α with more than one nonzero entry.

This reduces the problem to counting integer‑coefficient divisors of binomials \(1+t^n\) whose support lies in \(\{0,\dots,8\}\).
